items.readme:
# Doory Doory is a design editor that runs in the browser: posters, social posts, stories, slides, invitations, resumes, thumbnails and business cards. You start from a template or a blank page, edit everything on it, and export PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF, MP4 or GIF. There is no paid plan, you don't need an account to start, and you can run it on your own server with Docker or without it. It is a young project: the editor is complete, the template library is small (ten starter templates), and bug reports are very welcome.

## What it can do
Editing. Tools sit in a rail on the left and open as panels; the toolbar above the page changes with what you select. Animation. Enter, exit and emphasis animations, page transitions, music and sound effects. Present it, or export it as a video or GIF.
Layers. Rename, lock, hide, group and reorder anything, or right-click it to copy, duplicate and arrange. Share and export. One menu for share links, downloads and presenting. Downloads are made in the browser; print PDFs can have bleed and crop marks.
| | | |---|---| | **Text** | Headings, curved text, effects, font pairings, lists, an open-licensed font catalogue and your own fonts | | **Elements** | Shapes, lines and arrows, about 25,000 icons, emoji and illustrations, stickers, QR codes | | **Photos** | Upload, crop, masks and filters, background removal that runs in the browser, stock photo search with an Unsplash or Pexels key | | **Layout** | Layers, groups, alignment guides, snapping, rulers, several pages per design (each its own size), resize to another format | | **Motion and sound** | 27 enter and exit animations, 12 emphasis animations, 16 page transitions, 24 music loops and 88 sound effects (CC0), voiceover recording | | **Present** | Present mode with speaker notes, timing, auto-advance and a second presenter window | | **Together** | Share links that view, comment or edit (with an optional password), pinned comments, version history, real-time co-editing | | **Brand** | Brand kits with your colours, fonts and logos | | **Export** | PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF, MP4, WebM and GIF | ## Templates

Ten starter templates ship with Doory. Each one follows the layout of the best-selling templates in its category, uses open-licensed fonts and, where it has a photo, a CC0 one. Everything on them can be edited. Admins can add more in the admin site.

## Self-host it ```bash cp .env.example .env # set DJANGO_SECRET_KEY (openssl rand -base64 48) and POSTGRES_PASSWORD docker compose up -d --build docker compose exec api python manage.py createsuperuser # your admin account; nothing creates one for you ``` Open and start designing. The `web` container serves the app and forwards `/api` and `/ws` to the backend, so the browser only ever talks to one address.
The admin site (templates, users, content)
The admin site is at `/admin/` on your domain, e.g. . Log in with the account made by `createsuperuser`; accounts that only signed up on the site cannot open it. There you add and edit templates and their categories, manage users, designs and uploads, and look after fonts, element packs and audio. | To | Run | |----|-----| | Make an admin account | `docker compose exec api python manage.py createsuperuser` | | Reset an admin's password | `docker compose exec api python manage.py changepassword you@example.com` | | Make an existing account an admin | `docker compose exec api python manage.py shell -c "from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model as g; u = g().objects.get(email='you@example.com'); u.is_staff = u.is_superuser = True; u.save()"` | Without Docker, run the same `manage.py` commands with the `manage` helper from the guide below.
Add the starter content (templates, icons, fonts, audio)
A new site starts empty. Add what you want once it is running, or set the `DOORY_SYNC_*` and `DOORY_SEED_TEMPLATES` options in `.env` to `true` and the API container does it on start: ```bash docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_gallery # template categories docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_fonts --popular 100 docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_templates # the starter templates (add --update to refresh them) docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_elements # shapes and graphics docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_element_packs # icons, emoji and illustrations (download) docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_models # background removal model docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_audio # music and sound effects ```
Settings worth knowing (.env)
| Setting | What it does | |---------|--------------| | `SITE_URL` | The public address of the site, e.g. `https://doory.example.com` (no trailing slash) | | `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | The host names the site answers to, comma separated | | `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT`, `SECURE_COOKIES` | `true` behind HTTPS, `false` for plain `http://` | | `EMAIL_URL`, `DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL` | SMTP, e.g. `smtp+tls://user:password@smtp.example.com:587` (without it, emails are printed to the API log) | | `WEB_PORT`, `WEB_BIND` | Where the site is published (default `0.0.0.0:8080`) | | `INSTALL_CHROMIUM` | `false` skips the headless browser that server-side PDF export needs | | `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` | Turns on "Sign in with Google" | | `UNSPLASH_ACCESS_KEY`, `PEXELS_API_KEY` | Turn on stock photo search | | `USE_S3` and `AWS_*` | Store uploads in S3-compatible storage instead of a local volume |
Run it without Docker (a Linux server with nginx and systemd)
Doory is three pieces: the API (Django on gunicorn), the real-time server for live co-editing (the same code on uvicorn) and the web app, a folder of static files that nginx serves while it forwards `/api` and `/ws` to the other two. The files in [`deploy/`](deploy) set this up. These steps are for Debian 12 or Ubuntu 24.04 with the checkout in `/opt/doory`; the paths are easy to change. You need Python 3.12, Node.js 22 (only to build the web app) and PostgreSQL. **1. Packages, a user and the code** ```bash sudo apt install python3 python3-venv postgresql nginx git curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo bash - && sudo apt install nodejs sudo useradd --system --create-home --home-dir /var/lib/doory --shell /usr/sbin/nologin doory sudo mkdir /opt/doory && sudo chown doory:doory /opt/doory sudo -u doory git clone https://github.com/shaongitbd/doory /opt/doory ``` **2. The database** ```bash sudo -u postgres createuser doory --pwprompt # pick a password of letters and digits sudo -u postgres createdb doory --owner doory ``` **3. The API** ```bash cd /opt/doory/backend sudo -u doory python3 -m venv .venv sudo -u doory .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt sudo -u doory nano .env # paste the settings below ``` ```ini DJANGO_SECRET_KEY= # openssl rand -base64 48 SITE_URL=https://design.example.com DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS=design.example.com # add the server's IP to try it by address DATABASE_URL=postgres://doory:YOUR_PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:5432/doory CACHE_URL=dbcache://doory_cache MEDIA_ROOT=/opt/doory/media # Plain http:// while you try it out; remove both lines once HTTPS works. SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=false SECURE_COOKIES=false ``` Then prepare the database and add an admin account: ```bash manage() { sudo -u doory .venv/bin/python manage.py "$@" --settings=doory.settings.prod; } manage migrate manage createcachetable manage collectstatic --noinput manage createsuperuser ``` The starter content is added with the same commands as above, e.g. `manage seed_gallery`, `manage sync_fonts --popular 100` and `manage seed_templates`. **4. The web app** ```bash cd /opt/doory/frontend sudo -u doory npm ci && sudo -u doory npm run build # writes frontend/dist ``` **5. Start everything** ```bash sudo cp /opt/doory/deploy/doory-api.service /opt/doory/deploy/doory-realtime.service /etc/systemd/system/ sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now doory-api doory-realtime sudo cp /opt/doory/deploy/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/doory.conf # set server_name in it sudo rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default sudo -u doory mkdir -p /opt/doory/media # uploads; nginx serves them from here sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx ``` Open your domain. For HTTPS, `sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx && sudo certbot --nginx`, then remove the two `SECURE_` lines from `.env` and `sudo systemctl restart doory-api doory-realtime`. **Updating:** `sudo -u doory git pull`, then repeat `pip install`, `manage migrate`, `manage collectstatic --noinput` and `npm ci && npm run build`, and `sudo systemctl restart doory-api doory-realtime`. **Optional:** server-side PDF export needs a headless Chromium: `sudo .venv/bin/playwright install-deps chromium`, then `sudo -u doory .venv/bin/playwright install chromium`. Without it, set `SERVER_PDF_ENABLED=false` in `.env`.
Develop locally
```bash make setup # virtualenv, dependencies, local database make dev-api # API on http://localhost:8000 make dev-web # app on http://localhost:5173 (second terminal) ``` `make help` lists the other targets (tests, lint, content).
## FAQ
Is it really free?
Yes. Doory has no paid plan, no locked features and no ads.
Do I need an account?
No. Guests design straight away and their work is saved in the browser. An account keeps designs in the cloud, lets you share them and use brand kits; signing up moves your guest designs over in one step.
Can I use it for my business or host it for my users?
Yes, as long as you credit the author as the licence asks: keep the licence and NOTICE with it and show the credit in the running app. See License and credit.
Where are my designs stored?
Guest designs and their images live in the browser on that device. Signed-in designs are stored on the server that runs Doory: yours, if you self-host. Uploads can go to a local volume or to S3-compatible storage.
## Built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Fabric.js, Yjs and Zustand in the browser; Django 5, Django REST Framework, Channels and PostgreSQL on the server; Docker Compose with nginx, optional Redis and S3-compatible storage. ## Contributing Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome. Open an [issue](https://github.com/shaongitbd/doory/issues) to report a bug or suggest a feature. For a security problem, please report it privately through the repository's **Security** tab instead. ## License and credit Doory is released under the [Attribution Assurance License](LICENSE). You may use, change and redistribute it, including commercially, but **you must credit the author**: keep the licence and [NOTICE](NOTICE) with it, and display this credit prominently in the running app: > Doory by Siam, creator and maintainer of Doory — https://github.com/shaongitbd/doory Third-party software, fonts and content keep their own licences; see [THIRD_PARTY.md](THIRD_PARTY.md).


Made with care by Siam and the Doory bunny.

items.readme:
RustGIS

A fast, free and open-source GIS in pure Rust for mapping, analyzing and sharing geospatial data.
Native on Windows, macOS and Linux, and in your web browser. Your data stays on your machine unless you send it to an AI model you choose, and every action is a command you can script.

## Why RustGIS - **Fast and small.** One native program, drawn on the GPU, with no runtime to install and no server to run. - **Runs everywhere.** The same app on Windows, macOS and Linux, and compiled to WebAssembly at [web.rustgis.app](https://web.rustgis.app) with nothing to install. - **Local and private.** Your files are read and written on your machine, and nothing is uploaded on its own. The network is used only when you ask for it: web basemaps, plugins, the GeoLibre tools and the AI model you pick, which receives your questions and the data it reads to answer them. - **Everything is a command.** Every button in the ribbon is a command with an id. Script it from `rustgis-cli`, chain it in notebooks and models, or ask the AI Assistant to run it for you. - **Familiar.** A ribbon laid out in the order of the work (Home, Data, Style, Edit, Analyze, View, Publish), Layers and Browser panes, an attribute table, and undo for every change. - **Extensible.** Over 1,000 GeoLibre and Whitebox tools for terrain, hydrology, LiDAR and remote sensing, and sandboxed WebAssembly [plugins](docs/plugins.md) that add commands, tools and ribbon tabs. ## A tour

Symbology and tables. Selecting a layer opens its contextual tabs: symbology, effects, labeling and data. Selection is synced between the map and the attribute table.

AI Assistant. Ask about your data or tell the map what to do. The assistant runs RustGIS commands for you, and each change can be undone.

Analysis. A tool gallery, the Tools pane and a run history, guided workflows, ModelBuilder, and 1,000+ GeoLibre and Whitebox tools.

Rasters. GeoTIFF and COG of any pixel type, reprojected on the fly, with stretch, RGB, classified and shaded-relief symbology.

Globe and projections. A 3D globe, Equal Earth, Robinson, polar and regional presets, or any EPSG code.

Web basemaps. XYZ, TMS and WMS tiles, Mapbox Vector Tiles and MapLibre styles, on the flat map and the globe.

Layouts. Map frames, legends, scale bars, grids, map series and PDF export, plus reports and presentations.

Plugins. Browse and install sandboxed plugins from plugins.rustgis.app, each showing the permissions it asks for.

Dark mode and the View tab: effects, scene settings, panes and linked views.

Projects. Start blank, from the World Atlas sample, or open a .rgis project.
Every screenshot is RustGIS itself, rendered offscreen by `cargo run -p rustgis-ui-egui --example ui_shot`. ## Features | Area | Highlights | |---|---| | **Data** | GeoJSON, CSV/TSV with x/y columns in any coordinate system or WKT geometry, Excel and OpenDocument spreadsheets, GeoRSS, LandXML, encoded polylines, Shapefile (zipped too, in the browser as well), GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, KML/KMZ (with styles), GPX, GML, MapInfo MIF/MID, OpenStreetMap PBF, TopoJSON, AutoCAD DXF, LiDAR point clouds (LAS, LAZ, COPC) and geotagged photos in (large files read in place), files by their web address, every vector format GDAL reads when it is installed, and SQL queries and DuckDB databases through DuckDB Spatial when DuckDB is; PMTiles archives (web or file) and MBTiles files; GeoJSON, CSV, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, Shapefile, FlatGeobuf, KML/KMZ, GPX and WKT out; standalone tables; layer and map files, styles, templates and packages | | **Rasters** | GeoTIFF and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF (any pixel type, tiled or striped, compressed), ASCII grids, Zarr 2 and 3 stores (a variable at a time step, by folder or web address); reprojection from any EPSG code; Stretch, RGB, Classify, Unique Values, Colormap and Shaded Relief; DRA, band combinations, brightness/contrast/gamma; raster functions, indices, change detection, classification, georeferencing | | **Maps** | Multiple maps per project; a 3D globe; Web Mercator or any projection (Equal Earth, Robinson, Winkel Tripel, polar and regional presets, or an EPSG code); bookmarks, extent history, Go To XY; five offline basemaps | | **Web services** | WMS, WMTS, WFS, OGC API Features and ArcGIS REST (FeatureServer, MapServer, ImageServer, VectorTileServer) from their capabilities | | **Web tiles** | XYZ/TMS/WMS raster tiles, Mapbox Vector Tiles and MapLibre styles (sprites, patterns, expressions), cached and fetched in the background | | **Cartography** | Single symbol, unique values, graduated colours, proportional symbols; collision-free labels with placement, scale ranges and annotation; masking, display filters, aggregation bins, 2.5D extrusion; graphics and dynamic text | | **Editing** | Create, move, rotate, scale, merge, split and explode features; snapping, templates, elevation, traverse, topology rules; domains, subtypes, attribute rules, relationships, archiving; undo for everything | | **Analysis** | Selection by attributes (SQL) and location; Buffer, Clip, Erase, Dissolve, Summarize Within, Summary Statistics and more; viewshed, line of sight, IDW, shortest path, suitability modelling; ModelBuilder and scripts; 1,000+ [GeoLibre](https://github.com/opengeos/geolibre-rust) and Whitebox raster, vector, LiDAR, hydrology and terrain tools | | **Imagery** | Ortho and reality mapping, pixel classification (k-means, minimum distance, a trainable neural network), mensuration, hosted imagery tiles | | **Layouts and reports** | Page layouts with map frames, legends, scale bars, grids and map series; reports with groups, statistics, charts and subreports; presentations (HTML slideshow, PDF); notebooks (Jupyter in and out) | | **Sharing** | PNG export at any DPI; PDF; web map pages, OGC API Features collections, MapLibre styles, glTF scenes, locators; project, map and mobile map packages; offline areas with sync | | **AI Assistant** | Ask about your data or tell the map what to do in plain language, with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible model; also `rustgis-cli ask`, and an [MCP server](docs/mcp.md) (`rustgis-cli mcp`) for Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and other agents | | **Plugins** | Sandboxed WebAssembly [plugins](docs/plugins.md) add commands, tools and ribbon tabs; install them from [plugins.rustgis.app](https://plugins.rustgis.app) on the desktop, command line and web | | **Interface** | Command search (Ctrl+K), keyboard shortcuts, dark mode, a customizable ribbon and Quick Access Toolbar, linked side-by-side maps, 16 languages | The [user guide](https://rustgis.app/user-guide/) covers each area in detail, [Comparison](https://rustgis.app/comparison/) sets RustGIS beside GeoLibre, QGIS and ArcGIS, and [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md) lists what's next. ## Get RustGIS - **Web app**: open **[web.rustgis.app](https://web.rustgis.app)**. The same ribbon and tools, with the browser's file picker for data and projects, and downloads for Save and Export. - **Desktop**: download the app for Windows, macOS or Linux from [downloads.rustgis.app](https://downloads.rustgis.app) or the [latest release](https://github.com/opengeos/RustGIS/releases/latest) (see [Installation](docs/installation.md) for the files and first-run notes). - **Package managers**: `winget install OpenGeos.RustGIS`, `brew install --cask opengeos/rustgis/rustgis`, `yay -S rustgis-bin` (AUR), or `sudo dnf copr enable giswqs/rustgis && sudo dnf install rustgis` (Fedora). - **From source**: `cargo run --release -p rustgis` (Rust 1.90 or later). ## Quick start ```sh cargo run --release -p rustgis # the desktop app with the World Atlas sample cargo run --release -p rustgis -- data.geojson # open data (or a .rgis project) ``` Command line: every ribbon action is a command with an id. ```sh rustgis-cli commands # all command ids and parameters rustgis-cli render countries.geojson map.png --basemap ocean rustgis-cli run --sample \ --cmd 'gp.run={"tool":"countPoints","params":{"polygons":"Countries","points":"Cities"}}' \ --cmd 'layer.symbology={"layer":"Countries_Summarize","type":"graduated","field":"point_count"}' \ --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"out.png","dpi":192}' --save atlas.rgis rustgis-cli ask --sample "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP?" claude mcp add rustgis -- rustgis-cli mcp --sample # RustGIS as an MCP server for AI agents ``` See [Command Line](docs/cli.md) for more. Python: the same engine and commands in-process (`pip install rustgis`), and the app itself in a Jupyter notebook. ```python import rustgis s = rustgis.Session(sample=True) s.run("gp.run", tool="buffer", params={"input": "Cities", "distance": 100}) s.to_png("map.png") gdf = s.layer("Cities_Buffer").to_geopandas() ``` See [Python](docs/python.md) and the [getting-started notebook](apps/rustgis-python/examples/getting-started.ipynb) ([open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/opengeos/RustGIS/blob/main/apps/rustgis-python/examples/getting-started.ipynb)). ## Architecture Layered crates, each depending only on the ones below it: | Layer | Crate | Job | |---|---|---| | L0 | `rustgis-geom` | coordinates, extents, Web Mercator, geodesic distance/area, scale | | L1 | `rustgis-data` | features and typed attributes; GeoJSON, CSV, Shapefile; GeoPackage, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf providers; SQL where clauses; rasters and their coordinate systems | | L2 | `rustgis-map`, `rustgis-analysis` | layers, symbology, labeling, camera, basemaps; geoprocessing (on `geo`) | | L2 | `rustgis-tiles` | web map tiles: XYZ/TMS/WMS, Mapbox Vector Tiles, MapLibre styles, the tile cache | | L3 | `rustgis-render` | tiny-skia renderer, label placement, PNG export, fonts | | L3 | `rustgis-plugins` | sandboxed WebAssembly plugins and the plugin registry | | L3 | `rustgis-geolibre` | the GeoLibre tool suite as geoprocessing tools | | L4 | `rustgis-engine` | session, undo, command registry, sample project | | L5 | `rustgis-assistant` | the AI Assistant: a chat agent that acts through commands | | L6 | `rustgis-ui-egui` | the ribbon front end (swappable) | | apps | `rustgis`, `rustgis-cli`, `rustgis-web` | desktop, command line, browser (WebAssembly) | `cargo xtask ci` runs formatting, clippy, the tests and the layering check. Contributor and agent notes: [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). ## Sponsor RustGIS is free and open source, and stays that way. If it is useful to you or your team, sponsorship is the most direct way to keep development, hosting and cross-platform distribution going. - [**GitHub Sponsors**](https://github.com/sponsors/giswqs): monthly or one-time, billed through your GitHub account. - [**Buy Me a Coffee**](https://buymeacoffee.com/giswqs): a quick one-off contribution, no account required. See the [Become a Sponsor](https://rustgis.app/sponsor/) page for what sponsorship supports and for other, free ways to help. ## License and credits Licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). Sample data from [Natural Earth](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/) (public domain).

items.description: Your personal AI agent in your own Cloudflare account. Chat, memory, tasks, notes and scheduled reminders, deployed with one command: npx create-talorys@latest. Free-tier friendly, single-user, no telemetry.
items.readme:
# Talorys **Your personal AI agent. Your own cloud.** Talorys is a free, open-source personal AI assistant that runs entirely inside **your own Cloudflare account**. It chats with you, remembers what matters, manages tasks, notes and projects, and runs reminders and routines on a schedule — without any server, database or account operated by the Talorys developers. One person. One Cloudflare account. One command. One personal AI agent. ```bash npx create-talorys@latest ``` --- ## 1. What Talorys is - **A private assistant** — chat with streaming responses, Markdown and tool activity indicators. - **Memory** — durable personal facts and preferences you can view, edit and delete. Only the most relevant memories are sent to the model on each turn. - **Tasks, notes and projects** — full CRUD in the UI, and from chat ("Add a task to review my project tomorrow"). - **Automations** — one-time and recurring reminders, daily task digests and optional AI routines, delivered to an in-app notification center. They run on Durable Object alarms, so nothing has to stay online. - **Single-user by design** — no signup, no accounts, no teams. The installer sets the owner password. - **Works without AI** — tasks, notes, memories and reminders keep working if Workers AI is unavailable or your free quota is used up. ### Screenshots | Chat with tool activity | Tasks | | --- | --- | | ![Chat](docs/screenshots/chat.png) | ![Tasks](docs/screenshots/tasks.png) | | **Memory (dark mode)** | **Automations** | | ![Memory](docs/screenshots/memory.png) | ![Automations](docs/screenshots/automations.png) |

 

## 2. How it works ``` Browser ──HTTPS──▶ Cloudflare Pages (React app + /api Pages Function) │ service binding (no public URL) ▼ Private Worker (Hono router) │ getAgentByName("personal-agent") ▼ TalorysAgent — Cloudflare Agents SDK Durable Object ├─ SQLite: conversations, memories, tasks, notes, projects, │ automations, sessions, settings, usage ├─ Workers AI: @cf/zai-org/glm-4.7-flash (streaming + tool calling) └─ Alarms: reminders and recurring schedules ``` - The browser only ever talks to your `*.pages.dev` site. `/api/*` requests run a Pages Function that forwards them over a **service binding** to the agent Worker. - The agent Worker is deployed with `workers_dev: false` and `preview_urls: false`: it has **no public URL**. - Authentication and authorization happen in the Worker, not the frontend. - Chat responses stream as Server-Sent Events end-to-end. More detail: [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md). ## 3. Cloudflare services used | Service | Used for | Free plan | | --- | --- | --- | | Cloudflare Pages | Frontend + Pages Function | Yes | | Cloudflare Workers | Private API Worker | Yes | | Durable Objects (SQLite) | All data, scheduling alarms | Yes | | Workers AI | Chat model (`@cf/zai-org/glm-4.7-flash`) | Yes, daily allocation | Talorys does **not** provision R2, D1, KV, Vectorize, AI Search, Workflows or any paid service. ## 4. Deploy ```bash npx create-talorys@latest ``` The installer: 1. Checks Node.js (20.18+) and uses its bundled Wrangler CLI (any globally installed `wrangler`/`cf` is detected but not required). 2. Verifies your Cloudflare login, or **opens Cloudflare's authorization page in your browser**. 3. Lets you choose an account (if you have several) and an agent name. 4. Asks for an owner password (hidden input, strength-checked). It is hashed locally with PBKDF2-SHA256 and stored only as a Cloudflare secret. 5. Generates a 256-bit session secret and unique resource names (`talorys--agent`, `talorys--web`). 6. Deploys the private Worker (creating its SQLite Durable Object), stores secrets, creates and deploys the Pages project with the service binding. 7. Verifies the live deployment (frontend, auth endpoint, unauthenticated rejection, storage health) **without** running any AI inference. 8. Prints the real `https://….pages.dev` URL reported by Cloudflare. It writes a `talorys/` directory containing `talorys.json` (installation id, account id, resource names, URL — **no secrets**) and the deployable artifacts. Keep it for updates. **Interrupted?** Run the same command again in the same place. It reconciles what already exists: no duplicate resources, no password re-prompt if the password is already configured, and **no data is ever deleted**. Non-interactive installs: `TALORYS_OWNER_PASSWORD=... npx create-talorys@latest --yes --account-id ` (with `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` set if you are not logged in). ### Permissions Browser login uses Wrangler's standard OAuth flow — no Global API Key. If you use an API token instead, it needs: - Account › Workers Scripts › Edit - Account › Cloudflare Pages › Edit - Account › Workers AI › Read - Account › Account Settings › Read - User › User Details › Read (optional; shows your email) See [docs/deployment.md](docs/deployment.md). ## 5. Access Open the URL the installer prints, enter your owner password, and start chatting. Sign in from any number of devices — they are all the same owner. Manage sessions under **Settings → Security**. Forgot the password? From your `talorys/` directory: ```bash npx create-talorys@latest reset-password ``` This replaces the password secret and signs out every device. ## 6. Where your data lives All data is stored in a single SQLite-backed Durable Object (`personal-agent`) **in your Cloudflare account**. Talorys has no telemetry, analytics, tracking or advertising code and sends nothing to its developers. Cloudflare processes your data to provide its services — including running Workers AI inference on your chat messages and the relevant memories included in each prompt. Review Cloudflare's privacy policy and Workers AI terms. Security model and threat mitigations: [docs/security.md](docs/security.md). ## 7. What is free and what may cost money Talorys is designed to fit the **Cloudflare Workers Free plan** and never enables paid features on its own. It is not "unlimited free", though: - Free plans have account-level quotas (requests, Durable Object usage, a daily Workers AI Neuron allocation). Quotas are set by Cloudflare and can change. - When the AI allocation is exhausted, chat shows a clear message and resumes after the daily reset. Everything else keeps working, and your data is untouched. - If your account is on a paid plan, usage beyond included amounts is billed by Cloudflare under your plan. Built-in guardrails (adjustable in **Settings → AI**): max output tokens, max context tokens (older history is summarized), max tool calls and reasoning steps per request, max AI requests per day, and max scheduled AI runs per day. Simple reminders and task digests never use AI. The Usage panel shows local **estimates** and links to the Cloudflare dashboard for exact Neuron usage. ## 8. Local development Requirements: Node.js 20.18+. ```bash git clone https://github.com/rociiu/talorys.git cd talorys npm install npm run dev ``` `npm run dev` starts the agent Worker (`wrangler dev`, port 8787), the Pages Function proxy with its service binding (`wrangler pages dev`, port 8788) and the Vite UI (http://localhost:5173) in one terminal. It creates `apps/agent/.dev.vars` with a local password (`talorys-dev-password`, override with `TALORYS_DEV_PASSWORD`) and uses the deterministic mock AI provider, so no Cloudflare login is needed. State persists in `.wrangler/state`. Other scripts: `npm run build`, `npm test`, `npm run test:e2e`, `npm run test:pack`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`. See [docs/development.md](docs/development.md). ## 9. Back up your data **Settings → Privacy → Download backup** produces `talorys-backup.json` with conversations, memories, tasks, notes, projects, settings and automations (never sessions or credentials). **Import** validates the file and merges it in one transaction; importing the same backup twice is harmless. ## 10. Update From your `talorys/` directory: ```bash npx create-talorys@latest update ``` This redeploys the latest Worker and frontend to the **same** resources. The Durable Object namespace is never recreated (migrations are append-only), the owner password and sessions are kept, and schema migrations run automatically and transactionally on first request. Also available: `status` and `doctor`. ## 11. Troubleshooting | Problem | Fix | | --- | --- | | Installer stopped midway | Re-run the same command; it resumes. | | "did not pass its health checks yet" | New `pages.dev` sites can take a few minutes. Re-run. | | Permission errors | Use an account where you can edit Workers and Pages, or a token with the permissions above. | | Chat says the AI allocation is used up | Wait for the daily reset; or enable Demo mode in Settings → AI. | | Locked out after failed logins | Wait 15 minutes, or reset the password with the CLI. | `npx create-talorys@latest doctor` checks everything automatically. More in [docs/troubleshooting.md](docs/troubleshooting.md). ## Repository layout ``` apps/agent Private Worker: Hono API, TalorysAgent, tools, SQLite repositories apps/web React + Vite app, Pages Function (functions/api/[[path]].ts) packages/shared Zod schemas, types, recurrence/DST logic, password hashing packages/create-talorys The one-command installer (npm package) tests/e2e Playwright UI tests tests/smoke Optional real-account deployment test docs/ Architecture, deployment, development, security, troubleshooting ``` ## License [MIT](LICENSE)

items.readme:
# Mailcheap

Mailcheap is a self-hosted newsletter app on Amazon SES. Write an issue, send it to your list, publish it on the web. About $0.10 per 1,000 emails.

![Mailcheap overview](docs/screenshots/overview.webp)

[![Deploy with Vercel](https://vercel.com/button)](https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fmarclou%2Fmailcheap&project-name=mailcheap&repository-name=mailcheap&env=MONGODB_URI,ADMIN_EMAIL,ADMIN_PASSWORD,SESSION_SECRET&envDescription=Database%2C%20login%20and%20signing%20secret.%20ADMIN_PASSWORD%20needs%2012%2B%20characters%2C%20SESSION_SECRET%2032%2B%20%28run%3A%20openssl%20rand%20-base64%2048%29.%20Add%20SES%20and%20QStash%20after%20the%20first%20deploy.&envLink=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fmarclou%2Fmailcheap%23environment-variables)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **No support.** This is a one-time open-source release. Issues are off, and setup questions go unanswered. Fork it, deploy it, make it yours.

## Why

Newsletter platforms charge for every subscriber, every month. With your own SES account you pay for the emails you send: 10,000 readers and 4 issues a month is 40,000 emails, about $4.

Mailcheap is the rest of what a newsletter needs, in one small Next.js app: an editor, a list, signup forms, unsubscribe handling, bounce and complaint handling, stats and a public archive. One admin, no teams, no plans. Your list stays in your database.

## Features

**Write and send**

- Editor with a live email preview, slash commands, image uploads and boxes. Markdown and raw HTML work too.
- Checks before every send: subject, preview text, unsubscribe link, size under Gmail's 100 KB clip, postal address, verified domain.
- Test emails, scheduling, and sending in batches through QStash at the rate you set.
- Send in steps: start with your most engaged readers, then send to more.

**Grow the list**

- Several newsletters in one install, each with its own from address, reply-to and postal address.
- A signup form on each newsletter's archive, and a signup API with API keys.
- Confirmed opt-in per newsletter, off by default. Welcome email.
- Rate limits on signups, login, unsubscribes and the API, on by default.

**Keep it healthy**

- SES events (deliveries, bounces, complaints) and a suppression list shared by every newsletter.
- A send pauses itself when bounces pass 2% or complaints pass 0.08%.
- One-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058 `List-Unsubscribe` headers) and an unsubscribe page, with signed links.
- List cleanup, off by default: readers who ignored several issues get one "do you still want this?" email, then stop getting issues.
- Open and click tracking on your own domain, with link scanners filtered out.

**Publish and measure**

- A public archive for each newsletter: issue pages, author page, share images, sitemap. Optional custom domain.
- Overview with subscribers over time, emails per hour, and delivery, open, click, bounce and complaint rates.
- Campaign reports by mailbox provider (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, iCloud...).
- Contacts with search, status filters and CSV import from any platform.
- A domains page with each SES identity's DKIM and MAIL FROM status and the DNS records to add.

## Screenshots

| Editor | Campaign report |
| --- | --- |
| ![Editor](docs/screenshots/editor.webp) | ![Campaign report](docs/screenshots/report.webp) |
| **Contacts** | **Public archive** |
| ![Contacts](docs/screenshots/contacts.webp) | ![Public archive](docs/screenshots/archive.webp) |

<details>
<summary>Issue page</summary>

![Issue page](docs/screenshots/issue.webp)

</details>

All names and addresses in the screenshots are made up.

## What you need

| Service | For | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [MongoDB](https://www.mongodb.com/atlas) | Contacts, campaigns, stats | Free tier works |
| [Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/) | Sending | About $0.10 per 1,000 emails |
| [Upstash QStash](https://upstash.com/docs/qstash) | Background sending and scheduling | Free tier to start, then pay per message. One message sends 50 emails. |
| [Vercel](https://vercel.com) or any Node.js host | Hosting | Free tier works |
| [Upstash Redis](https://upstash.com/docs/redis) (optional) | Rate limits shared by every server instance | Free tier |
| [Vercel Blob](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob) (optional) | Image uploads in the editor | Free tier |

Without Redis, Mailcheap counts the same rate limits in each server instance's memory. That still stops a script hammering a form, but on serverless hosts the limits aren't shared between instances and reset on each deploy. Add Redis before you put a signup form on a busy site.

Without Blob, image uploads in the editor are off. HTML and Markdown campaigns can still use images hosted anywhere.

## Setup

Plan for about an hour, most of it waiting for DNS and for AWS to approve production access.

### 1. Database

1. Create a free cluster on [MongoDB Atlas](https://www.mongodb.com/atlas).
2. **Database Access**: add a user with a password and the "Read and write to any database" role.
3. **Network Access**: allow `0.0.0.0/0`. Vercel doesn't have fixed IP addresses.
4. **Connect > Drivers**: copy the connection string and add a database name before the `?`, like `...mongodb.net/mailcheap?retryWrites=true`. That's your `MONGODB_URI`.

### 2. Deploy

1. Click **Deploy** above.
2. Fill in `MONGODB_URI`, `ADMIN_EMAIL`, `ADMIN_PASSWORD` (at least 12 characters) and `SESSION_SECRET` (at least 32; generate it with `openssl rand -base64 48`). With shorter ones, Mailcheap refuses to start and the logs say which one to fix.
3. Open `https://<your-project>.vercel.app/login` and log in.

Sending is off until you finish the next steps, so nothing can go out by mistake. On any other Node.js host: `npm ci && npm run build && npm start`, with the same variables, behind HTTPS.

If you plan to use your own domain for the dashboard (like `mailcheap.example.com`), add it in Vercel now and set `APP_URL` to it. Links in your emails use `APP_URL`, so it should be final before your first send.

### 3. Amazon SES

Use one AWS region for everything below (the examples use `us-east-1`).

1. **Verify a sending domain.** In the SES console, go to **Identities > Create identity > Domain**. Use a subdomain like `mail.example.com`, so your main domain's email is unaffected. Keep Easy DKIM with RSA 2048 and add the 3 CNAME records SES gives you at your DNS provider.
2. **Set a custom MAIL FROM domain.** On the identity, open **Custom MAIL FROM domain > Edit**, use `bounce.mail.example.com`, and add the MX and TXT records SES shows. This aligns SPF with your domain.
3. **Add DMARC** if your root domain doesn't have one: a TXT record at `_dmarc.example.com` with `v=DMARC1; p=none;` to start. Gmail and Yahoo require DMARC from bulk senders.
4. **Request production access.** New accounts are in the sandbox (200 emails a day, verified recipients only). In **Account dashboard > Request production access**, pick Marketing, and explain that readers opt in, that bounces and complaints are suppressed automatically, and that every email has one-click unsubscribe. AWS usually answers within a day.
5. **Create a configuration set**, named `mailcheap` for example, under **Configuration sets**. Leave SES open and click tracking off: Mailcheap tracks on your own domain.
6. **Create an SNS topic.** In the SNS console, create a standard topic, like `mailcheap-ses-events`, and copy its ARN. Then switch it to signature version 2, which signs messages with SHA256 instead of SHA1: `aws sns set-topic-attributes --topic-arn <topic-arn> --attribute-name SignatureVersion --attribute-value 2`.
7. **Send SES events to the topic.** In the configuration set, open **Event destinations > Add destination**. Select hard bounces, complaints, deliveries, delivery delays, rejects and rendering failures, then pick Amazon SNS and your topic.
8. **Create an IAM user for Mailcheap** with this policy, then create an access key for it:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ses:SendEmail", "ses:SendRawEmail"],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:ses:us-east-1:<account-id>:identity/mail.example.com",
        "arn:aws:ses:us-east-1:<account-id>:configuration-set/mailcheap"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ses:GetAccount", "ses:ListEmailIdentities", "ses:GetEmailIdentity"],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

9. **Add the variables in Vercel** and redeploy: `SES_REGION`, `SES_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `SES_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `SES_CONFIGURATION_SET` and `SES_SNS_TOPIC_ARN`.
10. **Subscribe Mailcheap to the topic.** In the SNS topic, **Create subscription** with protocol HTTPS and endpoint `https://<your-app>/api/webhooks/ses`. Leave raw message delivery off. Mailcheap confirms the subscription by itself; refresh and the status turns to Confirmed.

The **Domains** page in Mailcheap now shows your domain with its DKIM and MAIL FROM status. Optional: in SES **Account dashboard > Suppression list**, turn on the account-level list for bounces and complaints too.

### 4. QStash

1. In the [Upstash console](https://console.upstash.com/qstash), open QStash and copy `QSTASH_TOKEN`, `QSTASH_CURRENT_SIGNING_KEY` and `QSTASH_NEXT_SIGNING_KEY` (and `QSTASH_URL` if you picked a region other than the default).
2. Add them in Vercel and redeploy.

QStash calls `APP_URL/api/jobs/...` to send each batch, so the app has to be reachable on the internet. Mailcheap checks QStash's signature on every job.

### 5. Turn sending on

1. In Mailcheap, create a newsletter. The from address must be on your verified domain, and the postal address shows in every email's footer (anti-spam laws require one).
2. Set `SENDING_ENABLED=true` in Vercel and redeploy.
3. Write a campaign, send yourself a test, then send. For a new domain, set a limit to reach your most engaged readers first, and use **Send to more** on the report once the first step looks healthy.

### Optional

- **Archive on its own domain:** add the domain to your Vercel project, then set `ARCHIVE_HOSTS=news.example.com=<newsletter-slug>` and redeploy. That domain serves only the archive and the unsubscribe page, never the dashboard, and the app domain's `/archive/<newsletter-slug>` pages redirect there.

  This is the safer setup: issue pages show HTML from your editor and from API keys, and on their own domain that HTML never shares the dashboard's origin. Without one, the archive stays on the app domain, where the sanitizer, the sandboxed frame and the Content Security Policy protect it.
- **Image uploads:** in Vercel, **Storage > Create > Blob**, connect it to the project, and redeploy.
- **Shared rate limits:** create a Redis database in the [Upstash console](https://console.upstash.com/redis) and add `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL` and `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN`.
- **Alerts:** set `ALERT_FROM` (like `Mailcheap <alerts@mail.example.com>`) to get alerts by email at `ADMIN_EMAIL`: spam complaints, paused sends, signup floods and rate limiter outages, plus every login, new API key and send. Otherwise they only show in the logs.

## Local development

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<you>/mailcheap.git && cd mailcheap
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # set MONGODB_URI, ADMIN_EMAIL, ADMIN_PASSWORD, SESSION_SECRET
npm run dev
```

A local MongoDB works: `docker run -d -p 27017:27017 mongo` and `MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/mailcheap`.

- Sending stays off locally unless you set `SENDING_ENABLED=true`. When the SES keys are empty, the AWS SDK falls back to your default AWS credentials (`~/.aws`), so the domains page can show real data.
- QStash can't reach `localhost`. To try a full send locally, run the QStash dev server (`npx @upstash/qstash-cli dev`) and use the URL, token and signing keys it prints.
- `npm test` runs the unit tests and `npm run lint` runs ESLint.

## Deliverability basics

- **Send from a subdomain** (`mail.example.com`), so a bad week doesn't affect your main domain's email.
- **Authenticate everything:** DKIM (Easy DKIM), SPF through the custom MAIL FROM domain, and DMARC on the root domain.
- **Only email people who asked.** Never import a bought or scraped list. If bots fill your forms, turn on confirmed opt-in.
- **Warm up a new domain.** Send to your most engaged readers first, and grow each send over a few weeks.
- **Watch complaints and bounces.** Keep complaints under 0.1% and bounces under 2%. Mailcheap pauses a send above 0.08% complaints or 2% bounces. Add your domain to [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com) to see your spam rate at Gmail.
- **Make leaving easy.** Every email has one-click unsubscribe headers and a footer link, which Gmail and Yahoo require.
- **Clean your list.** Turn on list cleanup in each newsletter's settings to stop emailing people who never open.
- **Keep emails under 100 KB**, or Gmail clips them and hides the unsubscribe link.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Required | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MONGODB_URI` | Yes | MongoDB connection string with a database name |
| `ADMIN_EMAIL` | Yes | Dashboard login, and where test emails and alerts go |
| `ADMIN_PASSWORD` | Yes | Dashboard password, 12+ characters. Changing it signs out every session. |
| `SESSION_SECRET` | Yes | Signs sessions and email links. 32+ random characters. Changing it breaks links in sent emails. |
| `APP_URL` | On other hosts | Public URL of the app. On Vercel it defaults to the production domain. |
| `SENDING_ENABLED` | To send | Nothing is sent unless it's `true` |
| `SES_REGION` | To send | SES region, `us-east-1` by default |
| `SES_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `SES_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | To send | IAM user keys |
| `SES_CONFIGURATION_SET` | To send | Configuration set that publishes events to SNS |
| `SES_SNS_TOPIC_ARN` | To send | SNS topic Mailcheap accepts at `/api/webhooks/ses` |
| `QSTASH_TOKEN`, `QSTASH_CURRENT_SIGNING_KEY`, `QSTASH_NEXT_SIGNING_KEY` | To send campaigns | Background sending and scheduling |
| `QSTASH_URL` | No | QStash region other than the default, or a local QStash dev server |
| `SEND_RATE_PER_SECOND` | No | Emails per second, 1 to 14 (default 10). Use 6 on a free Atlas cluster. |
| `ARCHIVE_HOSTS` | No | Archive domains, like `news.example.com=weekly,letters.example.org=monthly` |
| `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL`, `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN` | No | Shared rate limits |
| `BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN` | No | Image uploads in the editor (set by Vercel Blob) |
| `ALERT_FROM` | No | From address for alert emails, on a verified domain |

[`.env.example`](.env.example) has the same list with more detail.

## API

Create a key on the **API keys** page and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.

**Add a contact**: `POST /api/v1/contacts`

```bash
curl -X POST https://<your-app>/api/v1/contacts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAILCHEAP_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"newsletter":"weekly","email":"jane@example.com","source":"website","ip":"203.0.113.7"}'
```

- `newsletter` (slug) and `email` are required. `source` labels where the signup came from.
- `resubscribe: true` brings back someone who unsubscribed (never someone who bounced or complained).
- Pass your visitor's IP as `ip` to get the per-visitor limit of 5 signups per 10 minutes. Each key is also limited to 600 signups an hour.
- Answers `201` for a new contact, `200` if it already existed, with `{ id, status, created }`. When the newsletter confirms signups, `status` is `pending` and `inbox` links to the reader's email provider for your "check your inbox" message.

**Create a draft**: `POST /api/v1/campaigns` with `newsletter`, `subject`, `previewText` (optional), `html` or `markdown`, and `archiveSlug` (optional). Answers `201` with the draft's id and dashboard URL. Sending stays a click in the dashboard.

**List sent issues**: `GET /api/v1/campaigns?newsletter=<slug>` returns each issue's id, subject, preview text, archive URL and send date.

## How it works

- Next.js App Router, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS with shadcn/ui, MongoDB through Mongoose.
- **Send** picks the audience (active contacts, suppressions left out, most engaged first), creates one message per reader, and queues one QStash job per batch of 50. Each job sends through the SES v2 API at `SEND_RATE_PER_SECOND` and pauses the campaign if bounce or complaint rates pass the limits.
- Welcome and confirmation emails go out right away, capped at 100 every 10 minutes per newsletter.
- SES publishes events to SNS, which posts them to `/api/webhooks/ses`. Mailcheap verifies the SNS signature, updates the message, the campaign stats and the contact, and suppresses bounced and complaining addresses for every newsletter.
- Opens and clicks go through `/o/...` and `/c/...` on your app's domain. Clicks within 30 seconds of the send, or from known link scanners, don't count.
- Archive pages are static and refresh when you send or save.

## Support

There's none: issues are off and pull requests may not be reviewed. This is a one-time release, with no updates planned. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for what's built in.

# new-term-radar

[中文说明](README.zh-CN.md)

A daily report of the names that are starting to surge in AI: new models, products, tools and repos, caught where they are said first, before they show up in keyword tools.

Built for people who make pages, posts or products around new terms: SEO for AI tool sites, newsletters, directories, anyone who wants to know about "Strata" or "Seedance" the day it appears and not two weeks later.

## Why

A new name leaves a trail, in this order:

1. A lab or a well-followed account says it on X; a model enters Hugging Face's trending list.
2. One GitHub repo takes off on its own.
3. Directories and competitors add pages for it; someone registers a domain for it and the site starts to rank.
4. Your own site gets its first search impressions for it.
5. Google Trends shows the curve, days or weeks later.

Keyword tools read step 5. This radar reads steps 1 to 4 every day and uses step 5 only to check itself.

One example it was built around: [Niko1221/Strata](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata) was created on 2026-09-24 and had 7,700 stars nine days later. People were searching "niko strata" from 9/26, while no second repo carried the name and no keyword tool listed it. A single repo gaining 800 stars a day is the whole signal, and it is public.

## What it reads

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  X["① X accounts you follow"] --> M
  HF["① Hugging Face trending"] --> M
  GH["② GitHub: one repo taking off"] --> M
  SM["③ Sitemaps of other sites"] --> M
  NS["③ New domains that already rank"] --> M
  M["merge terms"] --> J{"name of a new thing,\nor a common word?"}
  J -->|name| R["report + radar.db"]
  J -->|common word| O["listed at the bottom"]
  GSC["④ your Search Console\n(optional)"] --> R
  R -->|14 days later| T["⑤ Google Trends check"]
  T --> H["hit rate per signal"]
  H --> R
```

| Signal | What it catches | Needs | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| ① X | Names the accounts in your list used for the first time in 60 days | AIsa key | $0.003 per account per run |
| ① Hugging Face | Models new to the trending top 50; quantised copies grouped under the base name | nothing | free |
| ② GitHub breakout | A repo under 14 days old averaging 200+ stars a day, or +400 since yesterday; adds the search variants people use ("niko strata") | nothing (a GitHub token raises the rate limit) | free |
| ③ Sitemaps | Words that several new URLs on a site share and its older URLs rarely carried | the sitemaps you list | free |
| ③ New sites | Domains registered and first indexed in the last 90 days that already rank for 20+ keywords | AIsa key | about $0.13 per query, weekly |
| ④ Search Console | Queries your site got impressions for, for the first time (fresh data) | your own Google token | free |
| ⑤ Review | Each lead checked in Google Trends 14 days later, against its own baseline; hit rate and days ahead per signal | AIsa key | $0.0012 per search variant |
| Keyword table | For the day's new names: the generic search terms behind them (what people do with the new thing), each sized and given a decision | AIsa key; GoAnyAPI key optional | about $0.15 a day for 5 names, $0.22 with GoAnyAPI |
| Name judge | A small model scores every term: the name of one specific thing, or a common word? | AIsa key | a fraction of a cent per run |

Prices are what AIsa charged in October 2026. With the example config (35 X accounts read three times a day, the keyword table for 5 names a day) a month costs about $15: $10 for the X reads, $5 for the keyword table. Read fewer accounts, or read them once a day, and it drops in proportion.

## The keyword table

A name is half of what you need. "SynthID Detector" has a short life as a keyword and belongs to Google; the job it does, "ai image detector", is what people keep searching, and nobody owns it. Each day the radar reads the new names once more and writes one table with both:

```
| Keyword | Type | Behind | New? | Est. searches/day | Started rising | Peak vs gpts | Peak day | Last 7 days vs the 7 before | Now | Decision |
| **photocraft** | name | — | yes | 12747 | 2026-10-05 | 97 vs 3.1 | 2026-10-09 | — | still rising | **prioritize** |
| **claude haiku 5.5** | name | — | yes | 1863 | 2026-10-07 | 100 vs 23.7 | 2026-10-08 | ×6.0 | still rising | **prioritize** |
| **ai image detector** | generic | synthid detector | no | 2537 | — | 87 vs 31.6 | 2026-10-04 | ×1.2 | flat | watch |
| **photoshop alternative** ⚠ | generic | photocraft | no | 244 | — | 61 vs 61.7 | 2026-10-08 | ×1.8 | flat | skip |
```

(a real run, 2026-10-12, shortened)

How it is made (`radar/usecases.py`):

1. **Evidence**: the most-liked posts that mention the name (X advanced search) and, for a repository, its README.
2. **Phrases**: a model reads the evidence and writes the keyword an ordinary person would type for each job it sees people doing, with a quote that backs it. A phrase built on another product's name ("photoshop alternative") is kept and marked ⚠: demand often hangs on the incumbent, and whether to use someone's brand is your call.
   With a GoAnyAPI key (optional, below) the radar also takes **Google Trends' related queries** for the name: what people really searched together with it. For SynthID Detector that gave "ai photo detector", "google ai detector" and "ai detector"; these rows carry 🔎. Queries that hold the name are listed as its long-tails ("photocraft download", "nano banana 2.1 vs pro"). Queries that are themselves the names of other rising things ("gpt image 2.5" beside "nano banana 2.1") are kept as leads of their own.
3. **Screen**: a second call scores how well the name answers each phrase, marks brands, and spots the names of other things; the loosely related ones are dropped. For Claude Haiku 5.5 it dropped all six proposed ("ai coding assistant", "github copilot alternative"); for SynthID Detector it kept all five.
4. **Volume**: Google Ads monthly searches for the rest, one batch call. Phrases under `min_volume` are dropped; most are.
5. **Trends**, twice per row: the term alone gives the shape (new or not, the day it started rising, the peak, the last week against the week before, what it is doing now); the term beside a benchmark keyword (`gpts` by default) gives the size.

Searches a day are estimates. A generic term's come from its own Google Ads volume, moved to today along its own Trends curve. The benchmark is then sized from those terms, and a name, which has no volume data yet, is sized against the benchmark.

Decision: **prioritize** = rose in the last 30 days, still up, at least `min_daily` searches a day. **watch** = rose but smaller, too early to read, or flat with steady demand of that size. **skip** = fading, or flat and small.

Each name is read twice, the day it appears and three days later, because on announcement day the posts are announcements and no use shows yet. The generic terms are kept as leads and reviewed after 14 days like the names.

What to expect from it, from the first eight names we ran it on:

- **The names rose; most generic terms did not, within five days.** PhotoCraft, Claude Haiku 5.5 and SynthID Detector all climbed clearly. Of the generic terms behind them, one moved: "photoshop alternative" ran about 80% above its level in the US for five days after PhotoCraft appeared. The worldwide daily series the table reads showed almost nothing of it (2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 2); a US daily series from another source showed it plainly. So a flat reading from the worldwide series does not prove a term did not move. With a GoAnyAPI key the bigger rows are read from the one-country series instead, where a rise is 1.5 times the earlier level held for three days; the same run then shows "photoshop alternative" as `still rising (US)`.
- The table's dependable use today is to tell you **which existing demand a new thing serves and how big it is** ("ai image detector", about 2,500 searches a day). Whether generic terms follow the names is what the 14-day review will show, and we have no result yet.
- For pure model releases (Claude Haiku 5.5, Nano Banana 2.1) the evidence was announcements and benchmarks, and the phrases proposed were weak ("ai coding assistant"). It works better for products and repositories that do one job.
- **Google Trends' last two days are not settled.** For unrelated terms they came back as 0 and then 100, which reads as a spike. Our first pass was fooled by exactly this; every reader in the code now drops those two days, and a rise must last two days to count.
- Google Ads volumes run about two months behind. Trends reads nothing reliable for terms under a few hundred searches a month.

Set `"usecases": {"per_day": 0}` or pass `--skip usecases` to turn it off.

## One key, and an optional second

Everything the radar needs goes through [AIsa](https://go.aisa.one/yansen-zhu): X posts, Google Trends and domain data (DataForSEO behind it) and the models that judge names and propose phrases. One key, pay per call, no subscriptions to X's API or DataForSEO.

> That link is a referral link: signing up through it supports this project. The radar works the same with a key from anywhere on aisa.one.

**Optional: `GOANYAPI_API_KEY`** ([goanyapi.com](https://goanyapi.com)) improves the keyword table in two ways, for about $0.07 a day: it adds Google Trends' related queries for each name, and it reads the curve of the names and the bigger generic terms (1,000 searches a month or more, eight rows at most) from 30 days of daily data for one country, settled to yesterday. Those rows show the country after "Now", as in `still rising (US)`. Without the key the table is built from the model's phrases and the worldwide series alone. The service is young (first released in August 2026); in our tests calls took 20 to 55 seconds and about one in ten failed, so the radar tries twice, reports a failure in the table and carries on.

Without an AIsa key the free signals still run (Hugging Face, GitHub, sitemaps, Search Console); the report then lists every term unsorted, because nothing judges which are names.

## Quick start

Python 3.10 or newer. The radar uses only the standard library.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zhuyansen/new-term-radar
cd new-term-radar
cp config.example.json config.json      # then edit: your X accounts, sitemaps, topics
export AISA_API_KEY=...                 # from https://go.aisa.one/yansen-zhu
python -m radar daily --out report.md
```

The first run builds its snapshots: yesterday's X vocabulary, star counts and sitemap URLs do not exist yet, so only GitHub breakouts (which need no yesterday) are reported. From the second run on, every signal reports what changed.

Two commands:

```bash
python -m radar sources --out sources.md           # ① only: X and Hugging Face. Run every few hours.
python -m radar daily --skip x,hf --out report.md  # everything else, once a day
```

`sources` writes a report only when there is a new name. `daily` with `--skip x,hf` lists what `sources` kept in the last 24 hours. If you run only once a day, use `python -m radar daily` and skip nothing.

Other flags: `--skip` takes any of `x,hf,breakout,sitemaps,newsites,gsc,review,judge,usecases`; `--new-sites` runs the weekly signal today; `--mail` sends the report (below); `--state DIR` moves the database and snapshots.

## What a report looks like

From a real run on 2026-10-12 (shortened):

```
### Candidate new terms (names first; terms you already cover are marked)

| Term | Signals | Name score | Known | Search variants | Examples |
| **gridcraft** | GitHub breakout storytold/gridcraft ★3178 (626/day) | 0.95 | none | storytold gridcraft | GridCraft: an open-source, cl… |
| **artex** | GitHub breakout mhtsec/ARTEX ★3353 (825/day) | 0.85 | none | mhtsec artex, mht artex | AI 自主渗透测试系统 … |

Other rising terms (judged common words): anatomy, math, iphone use

### ⑤ Review (terms reported 14 days ago: did they rise in Google Trends?)

| Term | First reported | Verdict | Days ahead |
| strata | 2026-09-25 | hit | 3 |
```

and from `sources`:

```
| **qwen image 2.1** | Hugging Face: new at #4, 2 versions | 1.00 | none | Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo (text-to-image, ♥569) |
| **ltx 2.5** | Hugging Face: new at #6 | 0.90 | none | Lightricks/LTX-2.5 (image-to-video, ♥7347) |
```

`daily` also writes `report.json` beside the Markdown, with everything the report was built from.

## config.json

| Key | What it is |
|---|---|
| `lang` | `"en"` or `"zh"`: the language of the report |
| `x_accounts` | `labs` and `bloggers`: X handles to read. Labs say names first; pick the bloggers your field's new terms spread through |
| `sitemaps` | Sites whose new pages you want to see. `index` is a sitemap, or a sitemap index when `shards` (a regex) picks which sub-sitemaps to read. `pause` is the seconds between requests to that site. `strip_locale` drops `/en/`, `/zh-CN/` prefixes so one entry in many languages counts once |
| `topics` | Name and regex: each topic gets its own section listing the leads, repos and queries that match |
| `known_terms` | Terms you already have a page for, or never want reported. A lead that contains one, or is contained in one, is marked and not kept for review |
| `stop_words` | Everyday words of your field, added to the built-in list (which is tuned for AI tooling) |
| `judge` | `model` (any chat model on AIsa) and `min_score` (0.5) |
| `breakout` | `window_days`, `min_stars`, `velocity_min` (stars a day), `delta_min` (stars since yesterday) |
| `new_sites` | `queries`: a name and a SQL LIKE pattern on the domain (`"%ai%"`), one paid query each; `weekday` (0 = Monday) |
| `review` | `after_days` (14) and `per_day` (5 leads a day) |
| `usecases` | The keyword table. `per_day` (names read a day, 0 = off), `model`, `benchmark` (the keyword sizes are compared with), `min_volume` (monthly searches a phrase needs), `min_daily` (searches a day for "prioritize"), `recheck_days` (3), `related` (use related queries when `GOANYAPI_API_KEY` is set), `related_geo` (`US`), `country_trends` (read the bigger rows' curves from that country), `country_min_volume` (1000) and `country_max` (8) |
| `gsc` | `site` (`sc-domain:example.com`) and `token_file`. Leave `{}` to turn the signal off |

Please read each site's robots.txt before you add its sitemap, and keep `pause` at or above its crawl-delay. The example config makes a few dozen requests a day in total, spaced by `pause`.

### Search Console (optional)

```bash
pip install google-auth-oauthlib
python scripts/gsc_auth.py gsc_client.json   # opens a browser once, writes gsc_token.json
```

`gsc_client.json` is an OAuth client of type "Desktop app" from Google Cloud Console, in a project with the Search Console API enabled. Then set `"gsc": {"site": "sc-domain:your-site.com"}`. The token is read-only and stays on your machine; `.gitignore` already lists it.

### Mail (optional)

`--mail` sends the report through [Resend](https://resend.com). Set `RESEND_API_KEY`, `EMAIL_FROM` (an address on a domain you verified there) and `RADAR_EMAIL_TO` (comma-separated). `pip install markdown` for the HTML version.

## Run it on GitHub Actions

`.github/workflows/radar.yml` runs `sources` every 8 hours and `daily` once a day, keeps the state in the Actions cache, and writes each report to the run summary. It is off until you opt in:

1. Fork the repository (a private fork is fine).
2. Remove `config.json` from `.gitignore` and commit your config. It holds no secrets.
3. Add the secret `AISA_API_KEY`; optionally `GOANYAPI_API_KEY`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, `EMAIL_FROM`, `RADAR_EMAIL_TO`, `GSC_TOKEN_JSON`.
4. Set the repository variable `RADAR_ENABLED` to `true`.

## How the pieces decide

- **Names in posts** (`radar/terms.py`): capitalised words, words with a digit (`Qwen3.8`) or inner capitals (`HyperFrames`); a number after a name joins it (`Opus 5.5`). A name two accounts used counts; a name one account used needs 100 likes and must be unmistakably a name, since a capitalised word is often just the start of a sentence.
- **Surges in sitemaps**: counted per distinct URL against the site's own baseline, so one page with a long slug cannot fake a wave.
- **The judge** (`radar/judge.py`): one chat call per 25 terms, each with up to three places it appeared. If the call fails the report still goes out, unsorted.
- **The review** (`radar/review.py`): a variant "rose" when its peak after the day we reported it clears its own earlier baseline by 2x and by 10 points. A word with an older meaning ("strata": rock layers, property law) has a high baseline and does not count; "niko1221 strata" going from 0 to something does. Trends' unsettled last two days are left out.

## What we measured, and what we have not

- The name judge (`gpt-4.1-mini`) was run on 170 terms an earlier judge had passed as names in our own daily use. It agreed on 149. Of the 21 it rejected, most were noise the earlier judge let through (sitemap path fragments such as `io.github.wxt invoice`, `asd`); about three were real names it missed (`synthid detector`, `veo`, `v4.1 flash`), in a test that gave it less context than a real run does. It passed none of 40 common words (`dashboard`, `pricing`, `today`).
- Hit rates per signal: not yet. The review needs 14 days per lead and ours has only begun. The one seeded check, Strata, came back a hit, three days ahead of its Trends rise. Your own report shows your numbers as they accumulate; treat any signal as unproven until then.
- The X signal is only as good as the account list. It will not see a name none of your accounts says.

## Known issues

- **New sites (2026-10-12)**: AIsa's validation for `post_dataforseo_domains_whois_overview_live` currently rejects the filter format DataForSEO requires, so this signal reports an error and the rest of the report is unaffected. It worked until 2026-10-06. Use `--skip newsites` to silence it until that is fixed upstream.
- The built-in stop words and the Hugging Face name cleaning are tuned for AI models and agent tooling. For another field, add `stop_words`.
- Search volumes are not in the report. The radar tells you a name is new; check volume and the top results before you build a page for it.

## Development

```bash
pip install pytest markdown
python -m pytest -q tests
```

The tests cover the logic (name extraction, scoring, the store, the reports) and call no network.
